Mini-Lesson

Islam: Worship

6 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Muslims live in every country and speak many languages. Can they really be one community?
  2. Mission 2Muslims stop to pray five times a day, wherever they are. What happens in those few minutes, and why?
  3. Mission 3A mosque can be a domed palace or a converted shop. What does every mosque need?
  4. Mission 4Does a Muslim's prayer count for more in a crowded mosque than alone in a bedroom?
  5. Mission 5Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's own words. How does that change the way it is read and kept?
  6. Mission 6Shi'a Muslims follow twelve Imams, and every mosque has an imam. Is that the same word for the same job?
Mission 1

Mission 1: Muslims live in every country and speak many languages. Can they really be one community?

Make a guess: Muslims live in every country and speak many languages. Can they really be one community?

Mission 1

The ummah

  • Ummah: the worldwide community of Muslims.
  • It is based on shared faith, not on race, nation, language or class.
  • Every Muslim belongs from birth or conversion, through the Shahadah.
  • The Prophet compared believers to one body: when one part hurts, the whole body feels it (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, paraphrase).
  • The first ummah was formed in Madinah after the Hijrah: migrants from Makkah and Madinan helpers became like brothers.
  • Importance: belonging, mutual support, and a duty to care for Muslims everywhere.
Mission 1Read the source

One community

> "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." (Qur'an 3:103, Pickthall)

> "The believers are naught else than brothers. Therefore make peace between your brethren" (Qur'an 49:10, Pickthall)

> "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." (Qur'an 49:13, Pickthall)

Q1 What does 49:13 say makes a person "noblest"?

Show answer

Conduct, not nation or tribe.

Q2 What duty does 49:10 give members of the ummah?

Show answer

To make peace between fellow believers.

Mission 1

Living as one ummah

  • Worship joins Muslims: all face the qiblah (the Ka'bah) in salah; pray in Arabic; fast in the same month; meet at Hajj in the same clothes.
  • Giving: zakah and sadaqah reach Muslims in need anywhere, e.g. after floods or wars.
  • Many communities: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims both see themselves as one ummah, with different schools, leaders and customs.
  • Shi'a Muslims add loyalty to the Imams of the Prophet's family as guides of the ummah; Sufi orders add bonds between teacher and followers.
  • Some Muslims see the ummah mainly as a spiritual bond; a few groups want one political state for all Muslims.
  • Challenges: divisions between groups and conflict between Muslim countries. Many Muslims see healing these as a duty (49:10).
Mission 1

The mosque: centre of worship and of the ummah

  • Masjid means "place of prostration" (sujud).
  • Worship: daily salah, Jumu'ah prayer and sermon on Friday, Qur'an recitation, Id prayers, i'tikaf in Ramadan.
  • Centre of the ummah: the Prophet's mosque in Madinah was a place of prayer, teaching, welcome for travellers and community decisions.
  • Today mosques run madrasahs (Qur'an classes), marriages, funeral prayers, food banks, advice, youth and women's groups, and open days for neighbours.
  • Praying shoulder to shoulder, rich and poor, shows equality before Allah.
  • Different communities: Sunni mosques; Shi'a mosques and husayniyyas for gatherings; Sufi lodges for dhikr.
Quick check
?A Muslim in Glasgow gives money at Jumu'ah prayers for families hit by an earthquake in Turkey, though she knows no one there. Which idea best explains her action?
Mission check

?A Shi'a family and a Sunni family from different countries pray side by side at Id in a London park, then share food. Which statement best explains why both see themselves as part of one ummah?

The ummah is built on shared faith and worship; it holds many cultures and branches, and is lived out daily in places like Britain.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Muslims stop to pray five times a day, wherever they are. What happens in those few minutes, and why?

Make a guess: Muslims stop to pray five times a day, wherever they are. What happens in those few minutes, and why?

Mission 2

What salah is

  • Salah (OCR: Salat): the second pillar; set prayer at fixed times, five times a day.
  • A duty (fard) for every Muslim from puberty who is of sound mind; exemptions include women during menstruation.
  • Different from du'a (personal prayer in one's own words;): salah follows set words and movements in Arabic.
Mission 2Read the source

Prostrate and remember

"But celebrate the praises of thy Lord, and be of those who prostrate themselves in adoration. And serve thy Lord until there come unto thee the Hour that is Certain." (Qur'an 15:98–99, Yusuf Ali)

"Establish regular Prayer: for Prayer restrains from shameful and unjust deeds; and remembrance of Allah is the greatest (thing in life) without doubt." (Qur'an 29:45, Yusuf Ali)

Q1 According to 29:45, what does prayer do for the person who prays?

Show answer

It restrains them from shameful and unjust deeds.

Q2 According to 15:99, how long should a Muslim keep serving Allah?

Show answer

Until death, "the Hour that is Certain".

Mission 2

Wudu: washing before prayer

  • Niyyah (intention) and "Bismillah" (in the name of Allah).
  • Sunni practice: wash hands, rinse mouth, nose, wash face, arms to the elbows (right then left), wipe the head and ears with wet hands, wash feet to the ankles; most parts three times.
  • Based on Qur'an 5:6: wash face, hands to the elbows, rub the head, feet to the ankles.
  • If no water: tayammum (clean earth or dust). After sex or menstruation: a full bath (ghusl).
  • Wudu is broken by e.g. using the toilet or deep sleep.
  • Significance: to come before Allah physically and spiritually clean; a time to leave behind distractions and sins.
  • Wudu must be done in the right order, with clean water, without waste.
Mission 2

Five times a day

  • Fajr: dawn to sunrise: 2 rak'ahs.
  • Zuhr (Dhuhr): just after midday: 4.
  • Asr: afternoon: 4.
  • Maghrib: just after sunset: 3.
  • Isha: night: 4.
  • Times follow the sun, so they change through the year; mosques publish timetables, and the adhan announces each one.
  • Rhythm: the day is framed by Allah, from waking to sleeping.
  • Shi'a Muslims usually combine Zuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha, so they pray at three times a day, but still pray all five prayers.
Quick check
?Which statement about the five daily prayers is accurate?
Mission 2

Direction, intention, place

  • Qiblah (OCR: qibla): all Muslims face the Ka'bah in Makkah. In Britain that is roughly south-east.
  • At first Muslims faced Jerusalem; the qiblah changed to Makkah (2:144), about 16 months after the Hijrah.
  • Facing one point unites the ummah worldwide: like rings round the Ka'bah.
  • Niyyah: the intention, made in the heart, to pray this particular prayer for Allah alone.
  • Clean place and clothes: often a prayer mat; shoes removed; body covered modestly (for men at least navel to knee; for women all but face, hands and, in many schools, feet).
Mission 2

One rak'ah, step by step

  • Rak'ah (OCR: raka't; CIE: rakʿah): one cycle of set words and movements.
  • Standing (qiyam): hands raised, "Allahu Akbar" (Allah is greatest). Recite al-Fatihah, then (in the first two rak'ahs) another passage.
  • Bowing (ruku'): "Glory to my Lord, the Most Great."
  • Standing again: "Allah hears the one who praises Him."
  • Prostration (sujud), twice, with a short sitting between: forehead, nose, palms, knees and toes on the ground: "Glory to my Lord, the Most High."
  • After every two rak'ahs and at the end: sitting, reciting the tashahhud (including the Shahadah) and blessings on the Prophet.
  • End: "As-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah" (peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah), turning the head right and left.
  • Significance: standing in respect, bowing in humility, prostrating in total submission: the moment Muslims say they are closest to Allah.
Mission 2Read the source

Al-Fatihah: the Opening

"Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds, The Beneficent, the Merciful. Master of the Day of Judgment, Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help. Show us the straight path" (Qur'an 1:2–6, Pickthall)

  • Recited in every rak'ah: at least seventeen times a day.

Q1 Which line expresses Tawhid in worship?

Show answer

"Thee (alone) we worship": worship belongs only to Allah.

Q2 What does the worshipper ask for?

Show answer

Guidance: to be shown the straight path.

Quick check
?During salah, at which point do Muslims say they are closest to Allah?
Mission 2Diversity

Sunni and Shi'a salah

  • Shared: five prayers, same rak'ahs, qiblah, wudu, al-Fatihah, ruku' and sujud, Arabic.
  • Hands: most Sunni Muslims fold their arms while standing; Shi'a Muslims (and many Maliki Sunnis) keep them by their sides.
  • Prostration: Shi'a Muslims prostrate on earth or something natural, often a small clay tablet (turbah), many from Karbala; Sunni Muslims prostrate on any clean surface.
  • Times: Shi'a Muslims usually pray at three times; Sunni Muslims combine prayers only on journeys or in special cases.
  • Wudu: Shi'a Muslims wash the arms from elbow to fingertips and wipe (not wash) the feet.
  • Words: Shi'a Muslims add a qunut (raised-hands du'a) in the second rak'ah and do not say "Amin" after al-Fatihah; their adhan adds phrases (see Mission 6).
Quick check
?Which practice is a difference between most Shi'a and most Sunni Muslims in salah?
Mission 2

Why pray?

  • Obedience: Allah commands it (4:103); it is a pillar of Islam.
  • Remembrance: "establish worship for My remembrance" (Qur'an 20:14, Pickthall).
  • Protection: it "restrains from shameful and unjust deeds" (29:45).
  • Cleansing: the Prophet compared five daily prayers to bathing in a river five times a day: no dirt remains (hadith, paraphrase).
  • Discipline and unity: the day is shaped by Allah; Muslims everywhere pray the same way towards one point.
Mission check

?On a school trip, Yusuf has no water nearby when it is time for Asr. He wipes his face and hands with clean dust, finds the direction of Makkah on his phone, and prays four rak'ahs on his coat. What best explains his actions?

Salah is portable: the duty stays the same everywhere, and Islam gives ways to keep it when circumstances change.

Mission 3

Mission 3: A mosque can be a domed palace or a converted shop. What does every mosque need?

Make a guess: A mosque can be a domed palace or a converted shop. What does every mosque need?

Mission 3

Masjid: a place of prostration

  • Mosque comes from Arabic masjid: "place of prostration" (sujud, bowing the forehead to the ground in salah).
  • Muslims may pray anywhere clean: the Prophet said the whole earth has been made a place of prayer for him (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase).
  • So a mosque is not needed for every prayer. It is where the community prays together.
  • The first mosques: Quba' near Madinah, built when the Prophet arrived in 622 CE; then the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah: a simple courtyard, walls of mud brick, a roof of palm leaves on palm trunks.
  • The mosque is a centre of worship and the centre of the ummah (the worldwide Muslim community) in each place.
  • A large mosque used for Friday prayer is a jami' masjid ("gathering mosque").
Mission 3

Outside: minaret and dome

  • Minaret: the tower from which the adhan (call to prayer) was traditionally called.
  • CIE: the minaret as the "site of light".
  • Dome: a symbol of the vault of heaven, of Allah's creation over all; it also carries the voice of the imam round the hall.
  • Neither is required. Mosques take the shape of their culture:
  • e.g. pagoda-style roofs at the Great Mosque of Xi'an (China); mud-brick walls at Djenné (Mali); terraced houses and former churches, chapels and shops in Britain.
  • What every mosque needs: a clean prayer space, a way to show the direction of Makkah, and somewhere for wudu (washing).
Mission 3

Inside: everything faces Makkah

  • Qiblah: the direction of the Ka'bah in Makkah. The wall facing it is the qiblah wall.
  • Mihrab: a niche in the qiblah wall. It shows the direction and marks where the imam leads prayer.
  • Minbar: stepped platform beside the mihrab, from which the imam gives the khutbah (sermon) at Friday prayer. The Prophet preached from a minbar of three steps.
  • Musalla (prayer hall): an open carpeted space, no seats or images; lines on the carpet keep worshippers in straight rows shoulder to shoulder.
  • Wudu area (ablution area): taps, seats and drains for washing hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head and feet before salah (see Mission 2).
  • Shoes are left at the entrance: the prayer space is kept clean.
Quick check
?Which feature of a mosque is matched with its correct purpose?
Mission 3

Men's and women's spaces

  • Most mosques have separate areas for men and women: a balcony, a side room, or a screen.
  • Reasons given: modesty; concentration during bowing and prostration in close rows; it follows the order of rows in the Prophet's mosque, where men prayed in front and women behind.
  • Men are expected to attend Jumu'ah (Friday prayer); women may attend but are not required to (see Mission 4).
  • Different practice: in some mosques women pray behind the men in the same hall; at the Ka'bah men and women pray in the same space.
  • Some British Muslims, women and men, criticise mosques with small or no women's areas and campaign for better facilities.
Mission 3Read the source

Ibrahim and the idols

Ibrahim (Abraham) asks his father and his people: "What are these images unto which ye pay devotion?" (Qur'an 21:52, Pickthall)

"Then he reduced them to fragments, all save the chief of them, that haply they might have recourse to it." (Qur'an 21:58, Pickthall)

  • The people say they found their fathers worshipping the idols (21:53); Ibrahim replies that their Lord is the Creator of the heavens and the earth (21:56).
  • When questioned, he points them to the largest idol, which cannot speak (21:59–63, paraphrase).

Q1 What does Ibrahim reject in this passage?

Show answer

Worshipping images made by humans instead of the Creator.

Q2 How might this story explain the absence of pictures in a mosque?

Show answer

Images could become objects of worship, which is shirk; so the prayer space has none.

Mission 3

Calligraphy, pattern, no images

  • Mosques contain no pictures of people or animals: nothing that could be worshipped or distract from Allah. Hadith also warn against making images of living beings (paraphrase).
  • Shirk (associating anything with Allah) is the gravest sin; Ibrahim's breaking of the idols (21:58) is its model rejection.
  • Instead: calligraphy (beautiful writing) of Qur'an verses, the name Allah, the name Muhammad, and in Shi'a mosques often Ali, Hasan and Husayn.
  • Styles include angular Kufic and flowing Naskh and Thuluth.
  • Geometric patterns and arabesques (plant-like scrolls) repeat without end: many Muslims see them as pointing to Allah's infinity and the order of creation.
  • Purpose: to express belief (Tawhid), honour Allah's words, aid remembrance, and beautify worship without images.
Mission 3

Objects used in worship

  • Copies of the Qur'an: kept on high shelves and read on a stand (rehal or kursi); many make wudu before touching the Arabic text.
  • Prayer mat: a clean space for each person's salah; the arch woven into many mats is pointed towards Makkah.
  • Compass (qiblah compass, now often an app): finds the direction of Makkah when praying away from a mosque.
  • Turbah: a small tablet of clay, often from Karbala, used by most Shi'a Muslims: they hold that the forehead should touch earth or something natural that is not eaten or worn.
  • Misbahah (prayer beads; also tasbih): 33 or 99 beads to count dhikr, e.g. SubhanAllah, Alhamdulillah, Allahu Akbar after salah.
Quick check
?In a mosque, a worshipper places a small clay tablet on the carpet in front of her before she starts salah. Which statement best explains this?
Mission 3

What happens in a mosque

  • Salah five times a day; Jumu'ah (Friday midday prayer) with the khutbah from the minbar; Eid prayers.
  • Madrasah: classes, often after school, where children learn to read the Qur'an in Arabic and learn about Islam.
  • Life events: marriages (nikah), funeral prayers (janazah).
  • Ramadan: shared iftar (meal to break the fast) and night prayers.
  • Community: food banks, advice, youth groups, libraries, and open days for visitors of other faiths and none.
  • Leaders: the imam leads prayer, preaches and teaches; the mu'azzin gives the adhan (both taught fully in Mission 6).
Mission check

?A small Muslim community in a seaside town buys an old shop to use as a mosque. They have little money. Which change is needed first so that they can pray salah together there?

A mosque can look like anything. What makes it a mosque is a clean space where people bow together towards Makkah.

Mission 4

Mission 4: Does a Muslim's prayer count for more in a crowded mosque than alone in a bedroom?

Make a guess: Does a Muslim's prayer count for more in a crowded mosque than alone in a bedroom?

Mission 4

Jumu'ah: Friday prayer

  • Jumu'ah (AQA, OCR, EDXA, EDXB, EDQ: Jummah; CIE: Jumʿah; EDXI: Jum'a): the Friday congregational prayer, held in place of Zuhr.
  • Form: a sermon (khutbah), then two rak'ahs led by the imam.
  • Who must attend (Sunni teaching): adult Muslim men who are healthy and not travelling. Women, children, travellers and the sick need not attend, but may; if they do, it replaces their Zuhr.
  • Preparation: a full wash (ghusl), clean clothes, arriving early.
  • Shi'a practice: during the Imam's occultation, many Twelver scholars teach that Jumu'ah may be prayed instead of Zuhr, not that it is required; large Friday prayers are held in Iran and Iraq, and in some British Shi'a centres.
Mission 4Read the source

Leave your trading

"O ye who believe! When the call is proclaimed to prayer on Friday … hasten earnestly to the Remembrance of Allah, and leave off business … That is best for you if ye but knew!" (Qur'an 62:9, Yusuf Ali)

"And when the prayer is ended, then disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty, and remember Allah much, that ye may be successful." (Qur'an 62:10, Pickthall)

  • Friday is not a day of rest like a Sabbath: work stops for the prayer, then continues.

Q1 What must believers do when the Friday call is heard?

Show answer

Hurry to remember Allah and leave business.

Q2 What may they do after the prayer?

Show answer

Go back to work and seek Allah's bounty, still remembering Allah.

Mission 4

The khutbah

  • Khutbah (OCR: khutba): a sermon in two parts, given by the imam from the minbar (pulpit); he sits briefly between them.
  • Contains praise of Allah, blessings on the Prophet, verses of the Qur'an and a du'a for the ummah.
  • Language: traditionally Arabic; in Britain usually partly in English or another community language, so all can understand.
  • Topics: faith, character, family life, current events, how to live as Muslims in society.
  • Worshippers sit in silence and listen: the khutbah is part of the worship.
Mission 4

Praying together

  • Rows: shoulder to shoulder, feet together, facing the qiblah behind one imam.
  • Equality: rich and poor, of every race and nation, stand side by side: the ummah made visible.
  • Reward: the Prophet taught that prayer in congregation is twenty-seven times better than prayer alone (Sahih al-Bukhari, paraphrase).
  • Mosque practice: men usually pray in front; women behind or in their own area or balcony; some mosques have no women's space, which many Muslims criticise.
  • Many Muslims pray all five prayers in the mosque; others go mainly for Jumu'ah, Ramadan and Eid.
Quick check
?Which statement about Jumu'ah is accurate?
Mission 4

Prayer at home and elsewhere

  • The Prophet taught that the whole earth has been made a place of prayer: any clean place will do (hadith, paraphrase).
  • Home: many Muslims pray most daily prayers at home, often on a prayer mat in a quiet room; families may pray together, with a parent leading.
  • The Prophet urged believers to pray some prayers (especially voluntary ones) at home, so that homes are not like graves without worship (hadith, paraphrase).
  • Elsewhere: prayer rooms at school, work, airports, hospitals; outdoors on a coat or mat. Travellers may shorten four-rak'ah prayers to two.
  • Women: prayer at home is fully valid; many women also attend mosques.
Mission 4

Du'a: calling on Allah

  • Du'a ("call"): personal prayer or supplication: asking Allah for help, forgiveness and guidance, or thanking Him.
  • Any time, any place, any language, in a person's own words or in prayers from the Qur'an and the Prophet; often with hands raised, palms up.
  • Preparation (CIE): being clean, facing the qiblah, praising Allah and blessing the Prophet first, being sincere and patient.
  • Special times: after salah, the last part of the night, while fasting, on Friday.
  • Content: e.g. "Our Lord! Give unto us in the world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good" (Qur'an 2:201, Pickthall).
Mission 4Read the source

"I am indeed close"

"When My servants ask thee concerning Me, I am indeed close (to them): I listen to the prayer of every suppliant when he calleth on Me" (Qur'an 2:186, Yusuf Ali)

Q1 What does 2:186 say about Allah's nearness?

Show answer

He is close and listens to everyone who calls on Him.

Q2 Why might this verse encourage private worship?

Show answer

Allah hears personal prayer anywhere, so no mosque or set words are needed.

Mission 4

Dhikr: remembering Allah

  • Dhikr (remembrance): repeating praises of Allah, aloud or silently.
  • After salah: "SubhanAllah" (glory be to Allah) 33 times, "Alhamdulillah" (praise be to Allah) 33 times, "Allahu Akbar" (Allah is greatest) 33 or 34 times, often counted on prayer beads (misbaha or tasbih).
  • Shi'a Muslims especially know this as the Tasbih of Fatimah, which the Prophet taught his daughter, and begin with Allahu Akbar (34).
  • Significance: "in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest" (Qur'an 13:28, Pickthall); it keeps Allah in mind between prayers.
  • Sufis make dhikr a central practice.
Quick check
?Which statement correctly shows a difference between du'a and salah?
Mission 4Diversity

How important is prayer? Different views

  • All Muslims agree salah is a duty; many teach it is the first deed judged on the Day of Judgement.
  • Abandoning prayer: some scholars (e.g. many Hanbalis) teach that deliberately abandoning salah takes a person out of Islam; most teach it is a very grave sin, but not unbelief.
  • Inner and outer: some stress correct performance; others, especially Sufis, stress khushu' (humble attention): a prayer without the heart is empty.
  • Mosque and home: some Muslims see the mosque as the heart of the community and attend every prayer; others pray mostly at home and go to the mosque on Fridays.
Mission 4Evaluate

"Praying in the mosque is more important than praying at home."

  • For: congregational prayer is "twenty-seven times" better (hadith). Jumu'ah must be prayed in congregation. The khutbah teaches and guides. The ummah is strengthened when Muslims pray side by side.
  • Against: the whole earth is a place of prayer, and Allah is "close" to every caller (2:186). The Prophet encouraged prayer at home. Sincerity matters more than place. For many women, carers and people far from a mosque, home is where they can pray.
  • Another view: they do different jobs: the mosque builds the community; the home builds personal faith and passes it to children.
  • Judge it by: What is prayer for? Does "more important" mean more reward, more duty or more effect on a person's life? Does it differ for men and women?
Mission check

?Hamza works nights in a hospital in Leeds. He prays Fajr alone in the staff prayer room, makes du'a for a patient in English, and goes to the mosque for Jumu'ah on his day off. What does his week show about Muslim worship?

Muslim worship works on different scales: alone, at home, in the mosque and with the whole ummah, each with its own place.

Mission 5

Mission 5: Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's own words. How does that change the way it is read and kept?

Make a guess: Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's own words. How does that change the way it is read and kept?

Mission 5

What the Qur'an is

  • Qur'an means "recitation": it is meant to be heard and recited aloud.
  • Muslims believe it is the word of God (Allah), in Arabic, revealed through the angel Jibril to the Prophet Muhammad from 610 to 632 CE.
  • It is the last of the revealed books (Kutub), and Muslims believe it is the only one kept exactly as revealed.
  • 114 surahs (chapters) made of ayat (verses; the word also means "signs").
  • After the short opening surah, al-Fatihah, surahs run roughly from longest to shortest, not in the order they were revealed.
  • Makkan surahs stress belief: one God, prophets, judgement. Madinan surahs add guidance for the community: worship, family, law.
Mission 5Read the source

Not his own words

> "Nor doth he speak of (his own) desire. It is naught save an inspiration that is inspired" (Surah 53:3–4, Pickthall)

  • The first words revealed were "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth" (Surah 96:1, Pickthall), in the cave of Hira'.

Q1 According to 53:3–4, where do the Prophet's words in the Qur'an come from?

Show answer

Not from his own wishes: from God's inspiration.

Q2 Why does this matter for the Qur'an's authority?

Show answer

If the words are God's, they carry God's authority, not a human teacher's.

Mission 5

The Night of Power and a gradual revelation

  • Muslims believe the revelation began on Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, in Ramadan: "Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Predestination." (Surah 97:1, Pickthall)
  • "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." (Surah 97:3, Pickthall)
  • After that night, it came in parts over about 23 years, often in answer to events, to strengthen the Prophet's heart (Surah 25:32).
  • The Prophet recited each revelation; companions memorised it and scribes wrote it down on parchment, palm leaves and bone.
Quick check
?Which statement about how the Qur'an was revealed matches Muslim belief?
Mission 5

Why the Qur'an has supreme authority

  • God's own words: for Muslims, not a book about God, but God speaking. It is the highest source of guidance and of Shari'ah law.
  • Unchanged: Muslims believe it is preserved exactly (15:9): the final, undistorted message.
  • Beyond imitation: "though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not" (Surah 17:88, Pickthall). Muslims see its language as a miracle (i'jaz).
  • In Arabic: "a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand" (Surah 12:2, Pickthall). A translation is treated as an interpretation of the meaning, not the Qur'an itself.
  • Complete: it confirms the earlier books and needs no addition.
Quick check
?Why do Muslims around the world recite the Qur'an in Arabic in salah, even if they do not speak Arabic?
Mission 5

Understanding the Qur'an: interpretation

  • Tafsir: explanation of the Qur'an by scholars, using Arabic, the Hadith, and the occasions on which verses were revealed.
  • The Prophet's Sunnah explains it: the Qur'an commands prayer; the Sunnah shows how (Surah 16:44).
  • The Qur'an says some verses are clear, "the substance of the Book", and others "allegorical" (Surah 3:7, Pickthall).
  • Different approaches: some Muslims keep closely to the literal meaning and the early scholars; others look for the principles behind a verse (justice, mercy) and apply them to new situations.
  • Shi'ah Muslims: the Imams of the Prophet's family are its most trusted interpreters. Sufis: look also for inner, spiritual meanings.
  • All agree the text is God's; they differ on how to read it.
Mission 5Read the source

Moral principles: Surahs 6 and 17

> "Say: Come, I will recite unto you that which your Lord hath made a sacred duty for you: That ye ascribe no thing as partner unto Him and that ye do good to parents, and that ye slay not your children because of penury" (Surah 6:151, Pickthall)

  • Requirements (6:151–153; 17:23–39, paraphrase): worship God alone; be kind to parents, especially in old age; give to relatives, the needy and travellers; protect orphans' property; give full measure and weight; keep promises; speak justly, even against relatives; follow God's "straight path" (6:153).
  • Restrictions: no shirk; no killing of children for fear of poverty; no adultery; no taking life except by right; no waste; no following what you have no knowledge of; no walking the earth in arrogance (17:37).

Q1 Name one requirement and one restriction from these passages.

Show answer

e.g. kindness to parents; no killing of children.

Q2 Why might Muslims see these as a summary of the moral life?

Show answer

They cover duty to God, family, the poor and society, and link to the "straight path": Shari'ah.

Mission 5

The Qur'an in daily life

  • Formal worship: al-Fatihah is recited in every unit (rak'ah) of salah; the Friday sermon is built on the Qur'an.
  • Informal worship: personal reading and recitation; verses used in du'a (personal prayer) and for comfort; many learn it by heart and become a hafiz.
  • Home: read daily by many families; recited at a birth, a marriage and a death; verses in calligraphy on walls.
  • Mosque: children learn to read and recite it at madrasah; in Ramadan many Sunni mosques recite the whole Qur'an over the nights of tarawih prayer.
  • Guidance: for decisions about family, money, food and conduct; with the Sunnah, the basis of Shari'ah.
  • Different views: some value recitation in Arabic as worship in itself, even without understanding every word; others stress study in their own language; most aim for both.
Mission 5

Treated with respect

  • Many Muslims make wudu (washing) before touching the Arabic Qur'an. They point to "Which none toucheth save the purified" (Surah 56:79, Pickthall). Some scholars read this verse as about angels and the heavenly book; most still see wudu as the respectful way.
  • It is kept on a high shelf, often wrapped in cloth, with nothing placed on top.
  • It is read on a stand (rahl), not on the floor; it is not taken into a bathroom.
  • Recitation begins by seeking God's protection from Satan (Surah 16:98).
  • Worn-out copies are not thrown away: they are buried or respectfully disposed of.
  • Many scholars apply these rules to the Arabic text more strictly than to translations.
Quick check
?Amira performs wudu before reading her Arabic Qur'an and keeps it wrapped on the highest shelf. Which belief best explains this?
Mission 5Evaluate

"Reciting the Qur'an in Arabic matters more than understanding it."

  • For: the Arabic words are God's own; translation loses meaning and beauty. Recitation is itself worship (Surah 73:4: "chant the Qur'an in measure", Pickthall). One Arabic Qur'an unites Muslims everywhere.
  • Against: it was revealed "that ye may understand" (12:2). "Will they then not meditate on the Qur'an" (47:24). Guidance only guides if it is understood; it is meant to change how people live.
  • Another view: most Muslim scholars say both matter: recite in Arabic and learn its meaning, through study, tafsir and translation.
  • Judge it by: What is the Qur'an for: worship, guidance, or both? Can a translation carry God's words? What do Muslims in different communities actually do?
Mission check

?Yusuf reads an English translation every day to understand it, but recites only in Arabic in salah. A friend says: "Then the English book is your Qur'an too." Which reply fits most Muslims' belief?

Because Muslims believe the Arabic words are God's own, the Qur'an is recited, kept and obeyed in ways no other book is.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Shi'a Muslims follow twelve Imams, and every mosque has an imam. Is that the same word for the same job?

Make a guess: Shi'a Muslims follow twelve Imams, and every mosque has an imam. Is that the same word for the same job?

Mission 6

One word, two meanings

  • Imam (Arabic) means "one who stands in front": a leader.
  • Every mosque has an imam: the person who leads the prayer and serves the community. Sunni and Shi'a mosques both have one.
  • For Shi'a Muslims, the Imams (capital I) are something more: leaders chosen by Allah from the Prophet's family to guide the ummah after him.
  • Belief in these Imams, Imamah (the imamate), is one of the Shi'a five roots of faith.
  • So the same word can mean a local prayer leader or a divinely chosen guide.
Mission 6

The imamate: who guides after the Prophet?

  • Shi'a Muslims believe Allah would not leave the community without a guide after the Seal of the Prophets.
  • No new prophet comes, but each age needs a guide to explain the Qur'an without error.
  • So Allah appointed Imams from the Ahl al-Bayt (the Prophet's household), beginning with Ali, his cousin and son-in-law.
  • Role: to lead, to interpret the Qur'an and Sunnah, and to be a perfect example.
  • Significance: the imamate continues the guidance of prophethood. Sunni Muslims see leadership as chosen by the community, not a root of faith.
Mission 6Read the source

Ghadir Khumm and "leaders who guide"

  • In 632, returning from his Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet stopped at the pool (Ghadir) of Khumm. He took Ali's hand and said: "Of whomever I am mawla, Ali is his mawla" (Hadith of the pond of Khumm, paraphrase).
  • Shi'a reading: mawla means master and guardian; this was Ali's public appointment as leader.
  • Sunni reading: most Sunni scholars accept the hadith but read mawla as friend and supporter: an honour for Ali, not a succession.
  • Allah told Ibrahim: "I will make thee an Imam to the Nations." (Qur'an 2:124, Yusuf Ali) Ibrahim asked for Imams from his offspring too; Allah replied that His promise does not reach wrongdoers (paraphrase).

Q1 In 2:124, who makes someone an Imam?

Show answer

Allah: Shi'a Muslims see the imamate as a divine appointment.

Q2 Why do Sunni and Shi'a Muslims read Ghadir Khumm differently?

Show answer

They understand "mawla" differently: guardian and leader, or friend.

Mission 6

What makes an Imam

  • Nass (designation): each Imam is named by the one before, by Allah's command. The community does not elect him.
  • Inerrancy ('ismah; OCR: infallible; EDXI: sinless): Allah protects the Imams from sin and from error in teaching. Shi'a scholars cite Qur'an 33:33: Allah wishes to remove all abomination from "ye members of the Family" (Yusuf Ali), read as the Ahl al-Bayt.
  • Knowledge: the Imams inherit the Prophet's knowledge and are the true interpreters of the Qur'an.
Quick check
?What does the Shi'a doctrine of nass teach about the Imams?
Mission 6

The Twelve Imams and the Hidden Imam

  • Ali (d. 661): the first Imam; his sermons and letters are collected in Nahj al-Balagha.
  • Husayn (3rd), killed at Karbala in 680: his stand against injustice is remembered at Ashura.
  • Ja'far al-Sadiq (6th, d. 765): a great teacher; Twelver law is called the Ja'fari school after him.
  • Ali al-Rida (8th, d. 818): his shrine at Mashhad, Iran, is a major place of pilgrimage.
  • Muhammad al-Mahdi (12th), born 869: Twelvers believe Allah hid him (the occultation), that he is alive and that he will return with Isa (Jesus) to fill the earth with justice.
Mission 6

Twelvers and Seveners today

  • Twelvers (the large majority of Shi'a): while the Imam is hidden, senior scholars (mujtahids; the most senior, marja', "source to follow") guide believers in his place.
  • Scholars disagree how far this reaches: some say into government (Iran's system of rule by a scholar); others say mainly religious guidance (many scholars in Najaf, Iraq).
Quick check
?How do Twelver Shi'a Muslims believe they are guided while the twelfth Imam is hidden?
Mission 6

The imam in Sunni Islam

  • Origins: the Prophet led the prayer himself and told others who should lead in his absence.
  • Chosen by the mosque community for knowledge of the Qur'an and good character, often after years of study.
  • Not a priest: no special holiness, no ordination; any adult Muslim man with knowledge can lead the congregation; most schools allow a woman to lead other women. Only Allah forgives sins.
  • Prayer: stands in front, facing the qiblah; the congregation follows his movements.
  • Community: gives the Friday khutbah (sermon), teaches the Qur'an, counsels families, conducts marriages (nikah) and funerals.
  • Shi'a mosques also have prayer leaders; Shi'a Muslims distinguish them from the twelve Imams.
Mission 6Read the source

Sahih al-Bukhari 73:34–37

  • 73:34: the Prophet held up two fingers together: he and the one who looks after an orphan will be as close as this in Paradise (paraphrase).
  • 73:35–36: one who works for widows and the poor is like a fighter in Allah's cause, or one who prays all night and fasts all day (paraphrase).
  • 73:37: young men stayed with the Prophet for twenty nights. He sent them home to teach their families, saying: pray as you have seen me pray; when prayer is due, one of you should call the adhan, and the eldest should lead (paraphrase).

Q1 According to 73:37, how is a prayer leader chosen?

Show answer

From among the group: here the eldest; no special class of priests.

Q2 What do 73:34–36 add to the imam's role?

Show answer

Leading the community in caring for orphans, widows and the poor.

Mission 6

The mu'azzin

  • The mu'azzin (CIE: Muʾazzin) calls Muslims to prayer five times a day with the adhan.
  • The first was Bilal, a freed slave of Ethiopian (Abyssinian) descent, chosen by the Prophet for his strong, beautiful voice.
  • Traditionally called from the minaret; a mu'azzin is chosen for a clear voice, correct Arabic and good character.
  • Significance: the adhan turns daily life towards Allah and gathers the community.
  • In many Shi'a mosques the adhan includes an extra line bearing witness that Ali is the friend (wali) of Allah.
Quick check
?Which statement about the imam of a Sunni mosque is accurate?
Mission 6Diversity

imam and Imam side by side

  • Sunni imam: chosen by the community · leads prayer, preaches, teaches · an ordinary believer with knowledge · many in every generation.
  • Shi'a prayer leader: the same role in Shi'a mosques, usually a trained scholar.
  • Shi'a Imam: appointed by Allah through nass (designation by the Imam before) · sinless and without error · the true interpreter of the Qur'an · twelve for most Shi'a (Twelvers), the last alive but hidden; a living Imam for most Isma'ilis (a smaller Shi'a group).
  • Different: for Shi'a Muslims, leadership of the ummah is a matter of faith (a root); for Sunni Muslims, a matter of practice and community choice.
Mission 6Evaluate

"The Imams are the most important source of guidance for Shi'a Muslims today."

  • For: Imamah is a root of faith. The Imams' sayings fill Shi'a hadith collections and shape Ja'fari law. Twelvers believe the Hidden Imam is alive and watches over the community. For most Isma'ilis the living Imam guides each age.
  • Against: the Qur'an is the word of Allah and comes first for all Muslims. The Prophet's Sunnah comes before the Imams' teaching. For Twelvers, day-to-day guidance now comes from scholars, because the Imam is hidden.
  • Another view: for Shi'a Muslims the sources do not compete: the Imams are the guardians of the Qur'an's meaning (the Hadith al-Thaqalayn joins "the Book" and "the family").
  • Judge it by: Which source settles disagreements? Does "guidance" mean law, example or spiritual help? Do Twelvers and Isma'ilis answer differently?
Mission check

?At a Shi'a mosque in Birmingham, a trained scholar leads the Friday prayer. A poster in the hall marks the birthday of Imam Ali al-Rida. A visitor asks: "Is the man leading prayer one of the Imams?" Which answer is most accurate?

"Imam" names two different things: a role any qualified believer can fill (in mainstream practice a man for a mixed congregation), and a divinely chosen guide in Shi'a belief.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • The ummah is the worldwide Muslim community based on shared faith (3:103, 49:10, 49:13), shown in worship, giving and care for others.
  • The mosque is the centre of worship and of the ummah.

Mission 2

  • Salah: set prayer five times a day (Fajr, Zuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha) after wudu, facing the qiblah, with niyyah and set rak'ahs reciting al-Fatihah.
  • Muslims pray to obey and remember Allah, to be cleansed and kept from wrong (29:45), and to unite the ummah.
  • Shi'a Muslims usually pray at three times, keep arms by their sides, prostrate on a turbah and wipe the feet in wudu.

Mission 3

  • A mosque (masjid, "place of prostration") is the centre of communal worship and of the local ummah; its key features face Makkah: qiblah wall, mihrab, minbar, musalla, wudu area.
  • No images of living beings; calligraphy and geometric patterns express Tawhid and reject idolatry (Ibrahim breaking the idols, Qur'an 21:58).
  • Objects: Qur'an on a stand, prayer mat, compass, turbah (Shi'a), misbahah.

Mission 4

  • Jumu'ah (Friday prayer) replaces Zuhr: a two-part khutbah then two rak'ahs in congregation (62:9–10); in Sunni teaching it is required of adult men.
  • Salah may be prayed at home or anywhere clean; congregational prayer brings unity and greater reward.
  • Du'a is personal prayer in any words or language (2:186); dhikr is remembrance of Allah, especially after salah.

Mission 5

  • Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's word in Arabic, revealed through Jibril to Muhammad from 610 to 632, beginning on the Night of Power.
  • For Muslims it has supreme authority; it shapes worship, home life and moral choices; it is handled with special respect.

Mission 6

  • Every mosque has an imam: a prayer leader chosen for knowledge and character, with no priestly status.
  • Shi'a Muslims believe in the Imamate: Imams appointed by Allah (nass), free from sin and error, beginning with Ali at Ghadir Khumm; for Twelvers the twelfth is hidden and will return.
  • The mu'azzin calls the adhan; Bilal was the first.
